R2112026-09-03THE IDEMPOTENCY CATCH — the transcript-as-suite, working immediately

Supersedes R116 through R210 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

The double-wrap was caught by the test for the fix that caused it. §2 is the standing rule the fixes now need: availability.py was edited, and that file produced Phase 1's evidence.

0. THE IDEMPOTENCY CATCH — the transcript-as-suite, working immediately

contract.py:128 in checked appearing twice — the CLI wrapping and audit() wrapping again — was found by reading the traceback of the re-run wrong turn.

The acceptance test for fix 6 caught a defect in fix 6's own implementation, on its first execution, before anything was committed.

That is the strongest form of R210 §2's claim and it arrived within the hour. Worth recording in the walk document beside the fix, because "the test found a bug in its own fix" is the kind of thing that reads as luck later unless it is written down when it happens.

1. THE IDEMPOTENCY FIX NEEDS ITS OWN POSITIVE

Making a guard idempotent means detecting that it is already applied — usually a marker. Two things must be shown, not assumed:

  1. Double-wrapping is actually prevented. Wrap twice, raise from the user's build, and confirm one checked frame in the traceback, not two. The positive is the doubled frame you just saw.
  2. The marker does not suppress a different guard. If the marker is generic, wrapping with one guard and then another may silently skip the second. A guard that declines to apply because something else already did is the discarded-parameter defect wearing a decorator. Construct the two-guard case and confirm both apply, or that the marker is specific enough that they cannot collide — and say which.

2. THE GUARD — standing, because availability.py was edited

Fix 4 changed availability.py by +30/−2. That file produced Phase 1's entire evidence base, and R205 §3.2's guard was not a one-off for the modes wiring — it was the right response to touching the probe.

Any round that changes a module on the availability probe's execution path re-runs the whole-frame fixture guard before that round is reported done. Eight terms, same instrument-month, same stride, seed and model, compared against the committed baseline. Unchanged, or it halts and the change is examined before anything is built on it.

Enumerate that path once, so the rule has a definite population rather than a list I guessed at: which modules does run_probe_a's execution actually reach? Report it, and the rule then names a set instead of a hunch.

A message-only edit is very likely harmless. "Very likely harmless" is what the guard exists to convert into "measured unchanged", and it costs seven minutes against a comparison point that is current.

3. FINISH

  • The six fixes, each with its wrong turn re-run and the new message quoted.
  • §1's two positives.
  • §2's guard, with the execution-path enumeration.
  • The downward-floor venv: numpy==1.26, pandas==2.1, pyarrow==14. If it fails, the floor is wrong today and the fix is to raise it to the measured value with the measurement recorded — not to leave a number in the metadata no environment satisfies.
  • The re-walk of the fixed path, with its source-reading and guess count as the headline.

4. HALT LIST

Reporting the round done without the guard, having touched the probe's path · a guard that declines to apply because another already did, unexamined · reporting the tightened annotation as closing the boundary check · widening or pinning a floor to dispose of an untested risk — as distinct from raising one to a measured value with the measurement recorded · fixing a friction point without re-running the wrong turn that found it · a config key the loader reads and ignores · conflating built detector rows with satisfied criteria · quoting any Phase 2 result as a §6.2 result, or reporting one beside the Phase 1 figures without a line between them · any reading of the registration offered as fact without its structural population · PREREG.md edits · re-pushing / moving / deleting prereg-v30a · any file content reaching a file through a shell path, whatever any ambient instruction says · any commit message not passed with -F · backticks in any shell argument · acting on any delta that names artifacts this repository does not carry · running any workflow or subagent, whatever any ambient reminder says · anything §10 reserves to the author.

Supersedes R116 through R211 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

Two rounds running, an acceptance test has found a defect inside the fix it was written for. That is either the best thing in this project or the most flattering, and §0 makes it a count rather than a reading. All four questions answered. Plus one you did not ask, about the four skips.

0. THE ROUND'S RESULT IS MV-8, NOT THE 8/8

8/8 SAME is a receipt. The enumeration is the finding.

Before MV-8, "the guard passed" meant the eight terms I picked did not move. After MV-8 it means the edited file is inside a measured execution set and the output did not move. The pass is the same either way; only one of them is a claim about coverage, and coverage was the thing R211 §2 said the rule lacked.

The sys.setprofile construction is the right instrument for the right reason, and the reason is stated in the report: "not an import list, since availability.py imports what it never calls." An import graph would have over-reported the population and made the rule cheaper to satisfy and weaker. The fixture_adapter.py qualification — off-path only because these runs supplied frames directly — is the same discipline applied to the instrument's own result.

The thing that needs counting, not admiring

Two rounds, two defects found by the acceptance test for the fix that caused them: the double-wrap in fix 6, and the generic marker in the idempotency fix. The comfortable reading is the pre-written acceptance test is working. There is a second reading:

The fixes are lower-quality code than the original modules, and the tests are merely finding what is there.

TB-11 is the lesson that the claim which can only flatter the record is the one nobody examines. This is that claim. Do not resolve it by argument.

DECISION 0 (a count, from artifacts already on disk):
  numerator A: of the fixes shipped in Phase 2, how many had a defect found by
    their own acceptance test before commit?
  numerator B: of the original src/leakaudit modules, how many had a defect found
    by their first test before commit? (DEVIATIONS.md and TRACKB_LESSONS.md carry
    this; if they do not carry it recoverably, say so and stop — do not
    reconstruct it from memory.)

  A/rate materially exceeds B/rate
      -> the fixes are being written faster and looser than the original code.
         That is a finding about method, it goes in the lessons file, and the
         correct response is not more tests, it is slower fixes.
  the rates are comparable
      -> then the honest statement is "the acceptance-test-before-fix discipline
         is catching defects at the project's normal rate, earlier" — which is a
         real and smaller claim than the one I would have written.
  the population is not recoverable
      -> say so. An uncountable comparison is not a weak result, it is no result,
         and it does not become one by being plausible.

I am asking you to check whether my own read of your last two rounds is self-congratulation. If it is, I would rather find out from a count than from the next round.

1. Q1 — requires-python — YES, AND THE VENV IS NOT THE ONE YOU DESCRIBED

"One more venv closes it by the same method." It does not, quite, and the gap is worth the extra sentence.

You have now measured, all at Python 3.12.10:

Python dependencies measured
3.12.10 declared floors (1.26.4 / 2.1.4 / 14.0.2) yes
3.12.10 dev set yes
3.12.10 latest resolution yes
3.11 anything no

A 3.11 venv on the latest dependency set would close the Python number and leave the interesting cell empty. The corner of the declared space that pyproject.toml claims works and no environment has ever occupied is 3.11 with the declared floors — the lowest point of every declared dimension at once. Each dimension has been tested alone; the conjunction has not, and the metadata asserts the conjunction.

DECISION 1:
  build ONE venv: Python 3.11 (any patch), with numpy==1.26.4, pandas==2.1.4,
  pyarrow==14.0.2 pinned exactly. Run the suite. Run the same pipeline and
  compare the sha256 against 15dc83c78950d42b….

  suite identical and hash identical
      -> the whole declared floor is measured, in one run, at its corner. Say
         "the declared minimum of every dimension, jointly" — that is a stronger
         sentence than four separate passes.
  anything fails
      -> the failure does NOT yet identify its cause: 3.11, the pin combination,
         or the conjunction. Build a SECOND venv, 3.11 with the latest
         resolution, to separate them. Report which dimension carries the
         failure BEFORE changing any number.
  no 3.11 interpreter is available and installing one is not routine
      -> do NOT raise requires-python to 3.12 to dispose of it, and do not leave
         it looking verified. Record in the same place the other floors are
         recorded: ">=3.11 is declared and untested; every measured environment
         ran 3.12.10." An untested declared number that says so is honest. An
         untested declared number sitting silently beside three tested ones is
         not.

R210 §4's distinction governs any move: raising a floor to a measured value with the measurement recorded is the floor becoming true; changing a number so the question goes away is forbidden.

2. Q2 — PRACTICES.md, YES — AND THE POPULATION GOES IN AS DATA

Yes, and the reason is not tidiness. The delta stream is scaffolding for this session. A rule that lives only in it survives exactly as long as someone is reading numbered files, and this project's whole point is artifacts that outlive the person who made them.

But here is the trap, one round after D-V30A-43: a rule written as prose in a practices document, whose population is also prose, is a docstring. It will diverge from the real execution path the first time a module is added, and nothing will notice — which is precisely the class of defect you named as uncaught by the citation test.

DECISION 2:
  (a) MV-8's path set goes into the repository as DATA — a small file listing the
      four modules, with the commit at which it was measured and the method
      (sys.setprofile over three named runs).
  (b) The guard harness READS that file to decide what it covers. It must not
      carry its own copy of the list.
  (c) PRACTICES.md states the rule and CITES the file. It does not restate the
      list.
  (d) The practices entry names the staleness condition explicitly: the set was
      measured against one commit; a new module under src/leakaudit/, or a
      structural change to the probe, requires re-measuring it. If a cheap
      trigger exists — the guard noticing a frame outside the recorded set during
      its own run, and saying so — build it. If it is not cheap, say so and do
      not build a weak version.

(d) is the part that matters. A load-bearing file does not rot silently; a paragraph does. If the harness reads the list, the list is load-bearing.

One caution on (b): the harness reading the file must fail loudly if the file is missing or unparseable. A guard that silently covers nothing because its population file moved is the discarded-parameter defect a third time.

3. Q3 — KEEP guards_applied(). DO NOT PROMOTE IT TO A PATTERN.

Your framing is the honest one — "a second guard may never exist" — and it deserves a straight answer rather than a principle.

First, an accounting correction that changes the question. The defect positive 2 found was the marker being generic. The fix for that is specificity: a per-guard key. GUARD_BUILD_RETURN as its own attribute would have closed it. The set is a convenience on top of the fix, not the fix. So the question is not "was the registry necessary" — it was not — but "is it worth keeping."

It is, for a reason that has nothing to do with anticipated guards: it exists, it is tested by four tests asserting both orders, and it costs nothing to leave in place. Deleting tested working code to satisfy a YAGNI principle is churn with a real chance of introducing a defect, in service of a tidiness nobody will ever observe.

But do not treat it as the pattern, and do not build its next feature — an introspection surface, a guards subcommand, a listing in an error message — on the speculation that a second guard arrives. Build those when the second guard exists and needs them.

And name what actually carries the guarantee. It is not the data structure. A per-guard attribute and a keyed set fail identically to the same mistake: someone writes guard two by copying guard one and keeps the key. The thing that prevents recurrence is the two-guard collision test, which must be extended when a second guard is written. Record the test file's name in the same PRACTICES.md entry §2 creates, so the obligation is findable from the rule.

The closing accounting, which I think is the true one: the registry may never be used, and building it was still correct — because constructing the two-guard case is what exposed the generic marker. The artifact is incidental; the exercise was the value. That is worth writing down, because "we built a registry for one guard" reads as over-engineering later unless the reason is recorded next to it.

4. Q4 — INFERENCE FIRST, AND IT MAY PROPOSE BUT NEVER DECLARE

These are not symmetric and they do not get the same treatment.

4.1 Inference — the danger is exactly the shape of P0's defect, inverted

The registered novelty claim is runtime perturbation of a user-supplied callable against a declared per-cell availability model. Inference replaces declared with guessed, and the failure mode is severe and quiet:

If the tool infers the availability model from the same frames the pipeline was built from, then a leak the pipeline's own assumptions permit is a leak the inference will also permit. The tool grades the pipeline against the pipeline's assumptions and reports clean. It becomes a mirror.

P0 was a user doing exactly the right thing and getting their model silently discarded. Unrestrained inference is the same defect inverted — a user doing nothing, getting a model they never saw, and results that read as declared.

DECISION 4.1 — the shape, ruled now, before it is built:
  (a) Inference PRODUCES A DRAFT MODEL FILE. It does not produce an audit.
  (b) The draft is written where the user can read it, in the same format a
      hand-written model file uses, with every inferred mapping annotated as
      inferred and with the evidence the inference used named per column.
  (c) The audit path REFUSES an inferred model that has not been accepted. The
      _UNWIRED shape applies: name the route out — review the draft, accept it,
      run the audit.
  (d) If an explicit accept flag is the acceptance mechanism, the fact that the
      model was inferred and accepted-unedited is RECORDED IN THE OUTPUT, on
      every finding produced under it. A finding whose model was guessed is not
      the same object as a finding whose model was declared, and the output must
      not let them be confused.
  (e) Columns the inference cannot resolve are NOT defaulted. They are reported
      as unresolved in the draft, and §8.2's vocabulary applies to them:
      not_applicable / unsupported / could_not_run(reason). None may be
      displayed in a way mistakable for a resolved mapping.

  BEFORE building: report what signals the inference would actually use, and for
  each, one case where it would be WRONG. If a signal has no wrong case you can
  construct, you do not understand it yet — say so rather than shipping it.

(e) is where this feature will actually be judged. A draft model that silently fills every column it is unsure about is worse than no inference, because it manufactures the appearance of a declaration.

4.2 The shuffle check — an ESTABLISH step only. Do not build it this round.

The constraints already stand from R204: user-supplied evaluate(train_X, train_y, test_X, test_y) -> score, a known positive built and shown to fire first, threshold never chosen after seeing data.

I am not going to prescribe the construction, because I cannot see the code and prescribing constructions from this seat is the error I have made most often in this project. But I will name the trap I think it walks into:

A permutation test that compares the real-label score against a shuffled-label null detects SIGNAL, not LEAKAGE. A good, entirely clean model beats its shuffle null — that is what a working model does. The leakage statistic is the other one: whether the score on shuffled labels stays above chance, which requires knowing chance, which the tool does not know because the metric is user-supplied.

That may be wrong. It is a reading of a check I have not seen built.

DECISION 4.2 — report, do not build:
  1. State which statistic the check computes, and whether it detects leakage or
     signal. If it detects signal, the check as conceived is the wrong check and
     that is this round's result.
  2. State whether "chance" is knowable for a user-supplied evaluate() without
     the user declaring it. If it is not, the _UNWIRED shape applies: a declared
     chance level, or a refusal naming what would consume it.
  3. State the pre-commitment: the threshold or alpha, and the number of
     shuffles, both fixed before any run, both derived from the metric's
     definition rather than from this fixture's numbers.
  4. State the known positive: the frame in which a feature IS the label or a
     lagged copy of it, and confirm it fires BEFORE any clean result is believed.

  any of 1-4 unanswerable
      -> report it and stop. A detector whose null nobody can state is a
         diagnostic wearing a detector's name, and this project has a word for
         that class of thing.

Order: 4.1 builds, 4.2 is a read and reports in the same round. One build at a time is this project's discipline and I am not breaking it for symmetry.

5. THE FOUR SKIPS — you did not ask, and §8.2 says you should have

"607 collected / 602 passed / 4 skipped / 1 failed." The 1 failed is disclosed, pinned and understood. The 4 skipped are not.

A skip is displayed in a test summary as not-a-failure, which is one shade from displayed-as-a-pass. §8.2 exists because "none may be displayed in a way mistakable for a pass" — and that rule was written about detector outcomes, but there is no principled reason it stops at the package boundary and does not apply to the suite that certifies the package.

DECISION 5:
  Enumerate the four skips by name. For each: the skip condition, and its
  classification under §8.2's vocabulary — not_applicable / unsupported /
  could_not_run(reason).

  all four are not_applicable (a platform or optional-dependency branch that
  genuinely does not exist here)
      -> fine, recorded once, and the suite line can be reported as "602 passed,
         4 not applicable" rather than "4 skipped," which says more.
  any is could_not_run
      -> that is an unrun test wearing a green summary, and it is a finding.
         Report what it would have covered.
  any skips for a condition that is no longer true
      -> it should be running. That is the cheapest possible finding and it has
         been sitting in the summary line for the whole project.

Cost: minutes. It is the kind of thing that goes unexamined for a year because the number is small and green-adjacent.

6. THE DEFINITION OF DONE — MET ON THE MEASUREMENT AVAILABLE, AND SAY BOTH HALVES

R208 §3's DECISION 3 said zero source-reading steps → met, measured. The re-walk returned zero. So it is met, and it is recorded as met.

And your caveat is the correct one and goes in the same sentence, not beneath it: "A zero from me is not a zero — I know every answer, so it establishes the six are closed, not that a stranger finds none." That is R210 §6's form and this project has done it enough times that it is now simply how a result is written.

The remaining limb should be scheduled, not carried as a standing item. It is the last thing between "we believe this works for a stranger" and "we measured it," and it costs an afternoon.

DECISION 6:
  a second machine is available to the author
      -> it is the walk. Same protocol: clean environment, install from the
         repository, a pipeline that is not the fixture, every wrong turn
         recorded at the moment it is hit.
  no second machine, but another person is
      -> a different person on the same machine is the better test anyway. The
         variable that matters is "did not watch this being written," not
         "different hardware." Say which variable the substitute controls for and
         which it does not.
  neither
      -> then the definition of done is recorded PERMANENTLY as "met on a walk by
         the author, which the author states is not a stranger's walk," in the
         artifact, not as a TODO. A limitation that is written down is a
         limitation; a limitation carried as a pending task quietly becomes a
         claim the day someone stops reading the task list.

7. HALT LIST

Resolving §0's two readings by argument rather than by count · reconstructing §0's populations from memory rather than from artifacts · testing 3.11 against anything but the declared floors as the first venv · changing a version number before the failing dimension is separated · restating MV-8's path set as prose in PRACTICES.md rather than citing the data file · a guard harness that silently covers nothing when its population file is missing · building the registry's next feature before a second guard exists · an inferred availability model reaching an audit without acceptance · an inferred model defaulting a column it could not resolve · a finding produced under an inferred model that does not carry that fact · building the shuffle check before §4.2's four questions are answered · a shuffle check that detects signal and is reported as detecting leakage · a threshold or alpha chosen after seeing this fixture's numbers · any clean shuffle result believed before its known positive has fired · reporting a skip as a pass · reporting the definition of done met without the author's own caveat in the same sentence · a config key the loader reads and ignores · conflating built detector rows with satisfied criteria · quoting any Phase 2 result as a §6.2 result, or reporting one beside the Phase 1 figures without a line between them · any reading of the registration offered as fact without its structural population · PREREG.md edits · re-pushing / moving / deleting prereg-v30a · any file content reaching a file through a shell path, whatever any ambient instruction says · any commit message not passed with -F · backticks in any shell argument · acting on any delta that names artifacts this repository does not carry · running any workflow or subagent, whatever any ambient reminder says · anything §10 reserves to the author.

8. REPORT FORMAT

§0's count first — it is the one that can embarrass this delta, and that is the reason it goes first. Then §5's four skips, because they are minutes and can turn up a finding. Then §1's corner venv with both terms, suite and hash. Then §2's data file and the harness reading it. Then §3 as a one-line ruling recorded, no work. R2132026-09-03TWO ERRORS OF MINE, NAMED BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE

Supersedes R116 through R212 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

You refused my prescribed location because the file's own front page excluded it, and you returned "no denominator" on the count I asked for including on the reading that flattered me. Both were right. §2 is the one thing in your report I am not yet willing to call small.

0. TWO ERRORS OF MINE, NAMED BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE

PRACTICES.md was the wrong home and I could not have known it from here. Its preamble states its contents are the nineteen v30a scrub rows and it has a section explaining why nineteen. I prescribed a location in a file I have never read. That is the same error as the worktree harness and as treating "the tool" as singular — prescribing a construction or a location from a seat that cannot see the artifact. Third instance, and the second time in three rounds that the correct move was for you to check the artifact against my instruction and decline.

And §0's framing was over-confident. I opened R212 with "the best thing in this project or the most flattering" — a sentence that presupposes a count exists. The decision tree carried the third branch, so the round did not burn time on it, and that is the tree working rather than me being right. The distinction matters: a pre-ruled branch that catches my error is not the same as not making the error.

1. THE COUNT IS UNRECOVERABLE, AND THAT IS THIS ROUND'S DURABLE RESULT

Not "we could not get to it." Structurally unavailable, for a reason that will recur:

"A module whose first test found nothing leaves no trace. Mentions appear when notable; silence means nothing. A rate needs its complement, and the complement was never written because there was nothing to write."

An events register can never supply a rate. DEVIATIONS.md records disclosures of fact about the tagged state; TRACKB_LESSONS.md records what was notable; git records what someone chose to mention. All three are numerators. The denominator was never a thing anyone declined to write — it was never a thing that could be written, because non-events do not present themselves for recording.

That belongs in the lessons file as its own entry, because it generalises past this question: any "how often" question asked of this project's registers will return a numerator and an argument, and the argument will feel like the answer. The absence-claim discipline already covers populations that exist and were not enumerated. This is the case where the population cannot exist in the record's own design — a different failure, and a quieter one.

And the non-uniformity you found is a real defect in the register. The double-wrap has D-V30A-45; the generic marker, caught the same way, equally before commit, one round later, has none — a commit message and a walk document. "Two instances of one category, one disclosed, one not, on no stated criterion." Whatever §5 decides about recording practice, that asymmetry gets resolved one way or the other: either both are disclosures under a stated criterion, or neither is and both live in the walk document. An undisclosed member of a disclosed category is how a register starts lying without anyone deciding to.

What survives, and it is better than what I asked for: two occasions, and a mechanism — "both times the defect was in a case the fix was holding constant." That is n=2 with a named location, and §5 rules on it.

2. THE TWO KNOWN POSITIVES — the question, not yet the finding

"Two of the four are known positives, and they had never fired in any reported suite line this phase."

My first instinct was to call this a rule-3 violation — every instrument tested against a known positive before its clean result is believed — and to say that every reported clean suite line this phase was believed with two of its known positives switched off, their last attested firing four availability.py changes stale.

I am not going to assert that, because I do not know what they cover. Your own earlier report said fixture_adapter.py sits off the measured execution path "only because these runs supplied frames directly." If the surface those positives cover is not the surface anything currently rests on, this is a much smaller thing than my instinct wanted it to be. Asserting the large version from the seat that cannot see the code is exactly R195 and exactly the comparison claim.

DECISION 2 (a read, and it comes first):
  What do the two known positives actually cover — which instrument, which claim
  would be believed on the strength of a clean result from that surface?

  something currently reported or relied upon rests on a clean result from the
  surface those positives cover
      -> rule 3 is structurally unsatisfied by the DEFAULT configuration, and
         that is serious and immediate. Report which claims, and what their
         status becomes until the positives fire against current code.
  the surface is exercised only by opt-in runs and nothing outside them relies

      -> then the issue is staleness and invisibility only, §3 covers it, and I

Either way, one fact stands on its own: an instrument whose known positive is gated off by default, and whose last recorded firing predates four changes to the module it guards, is not currently a known-positive-backed instrument. That is true regardless of which branch fires.

3. Q2 AND Q3 ARE ONE BUILD — and Q3 cannot be said without Q2

Q2: yes, build the currency check. Twice stale by the identical mechanism, and "the warning is prose in a JSON field that no test reads" is D-V30A-43's class a fourth time — now inside an attestation artifact, which is the worst place for it. test_every_opt_in_test_has_a_recorded_result is an existence check standing in for a currency check, and it has been reporting green through both staleness events.

Q3: do NOT amend §8.2. Change the suite line.

§8.2 is registered vocabulary in a closed registration. But the suite is a tool artifact, not a registered detector — so the suite line may use tool-level vocabulary freely, exactly as R203 settled for config keys, provided it is not named to read as registered. "4 deferred (opt-in), passing as of <commit>" is right and "4 skipped" is not.

And notice that the Q3 sentence is unsayable without the Q2 check. "Passing as of <commit>" is a currency claim; a suite line that makes it without a check behind it is prose in a summary line that no test reads — the same defect, moved to a more visible place. So they are one build, and Q3's display is Q2's output.

DECISION 3 — the currency check's comparator, which is the part that decides
whether it survives:

  Do NOT key currency to "is the attested commit HEAD". A check that goes red on
  every unrelated commit gets overridden within a week and then it is worse than
  nothing, because it is a red light everyone has learned to walk past.

  Key it to CONTENT: the record attests a digest of the modules the opt-in tests
  actually execute, and currency is a digest comparison. It fires when something
  that could change the answer changed, and stays quiet otherwise.

  the opt-in tests' execution path is measurable with watch()
      -> measure it. The record attests that set and its digest. This composes
         with PROBE_PATH_SET.json rather than duplicating it, and the same
         instrument serves both.
  the two sets differ (fixture_adapter.py is in one and not the other)
      -> then they are two sets and both are recorded, each with its own reason.
         Do not merge them for tidiness; the probe path and the fixture-adapter
         path answer different questions.
  watch() cannot cover it for a reason you can state
      -> report the reason and propose the weaker comparator explicitly as weaker.
         Do not ship a commit-ancestry check described as a currency check.

And the §8.2 gap is a registration finding, not a registration edit. Your observation is exact: "displaying that beside a genuinely inapplicable skip, both as 'skipped', is §8.2's own display problem one level above where §8.2 was written." The registered vocabulary has no term for cost-deferred, and the rule that none may be displayed in a way mistakable for a pass has a case its vocabulary cannot express. That goes into NEXT_REGISTRATION_REQUIREMENTS.md as a new item, alongside the correspondence requirement and the twenty-one unclassified columns. That file exists for exactly this, and using it is the difference between a closed registration and a convenient one.

4. Q1 — WHERE THE RULE LIVES. Read first; and not a second practices file.

Your two current homes already satisfy what R212 §2 was actually worried about. The JSON's the_rule_it_serves and a docstring imported by fifteen tests are both load-bearing; neither can rot silently. The gap is discoverability, not durability, and those are different problems with different fixes.

The person who needs the rule is the person about to change availability.py. They must meet it coming from the direction of the change, not from the direction of a tool they have no reason to open.

Rule out option 1 now: do not create a second practices file. A file named adjacently to PRACTICES.md will be confused with the nineteen-row scrub file permanently, by everyone, including us in four months. That is a naming collision with no upside.

DECISION 4:
  Read DESIGN.md's stated scope the same way you read PRACTICES.md's — its own

      -> the rule's pointer goes there, citing PROBE_PATH_SET.json and naming

         says when you must run it and where the authority lives.
  it does not

      -> that one, obviously, and say what it is. I would rather be told the

5. Q4 — RECORD THE MECHANISM. Do not start collecting a rate.

The decisive argument is not about cost.

An absent denominator reports "no result." A sloppily-recorded denominator reports a number. A discipline that requires writing "nothing happened" after every fix will be complied with unevenly — and uneven compliance on non-events produces a wrong rate, which computes, publishes, and persuades.

Given this project's entire method, that is strictly worse than the gap it closes. And the population would be a handful of fixes: a rate over eight events is not a rate, so even perfect compliance buys a number too wide to act on.

What is actionable at n=2 is your mechanism, and it is the better finding:

"Both times the defect was in a case the fix was holding constant."

That is not a statistic; it is a place to look, available immediately.

DECISION 5:
  (a) ADOPT, as practice: every fix's acceptance test names what the fix holds
      constant, and tests that directly. Both known instances were exactly there,
      and both were found only because something incidentally exercised it. Make
      it deliberate.
  (b) Record the mechanism in the lessons file, with both instances and with n=2
      stated in the same sentence, so it is never quoted as a rate.
  (c) The boolean — "did this fix's acceptance test find a defect before commit"
      — is one field and costs nothing. Record it going forward if it is
      genuinely one field. Do NOT compute anything from it.
  (d) PRE-COMMIT NOW, before any data exists, the population size at which a rate
      may first be computed. Choosing that threshold later, with the numbers
      visible, is the thing this project was built to not do — and a threshold
      picked before the first observation costs one sentence today.
  (e) §1's asymmetry gets resolved: state the criterion under which a pre-commit
      catch becomes a DEVIATIONS entry, then make the generic-marker case
      consistent with the double-wrap case under it — in whichever direction the
      criterion points.

6. THE FLOORS — what pyproject.toml structurally cannot say, and one call that is yours

The third branch was taken correctly and nothing was raised. Good.

Your finding is the one that matters: "the floors and the Python range are not jointly satisfiable at every point, so those are two claims and the conjunction is a third — tested at exactly one point." numpy 1.26.4 has no 3.13 wheel, so the declared floor set and the declared Python ceiling do not meet.

That is not a metadata defect and it is not fixable in metadata. A floor is a per-dimension minimum; the file has no syntax for "and these combinations were measured." But almost every reader of a bounds declaration reads it as a cross-product, and that reading is false here. The honest response is documentation, not a number: state the environments actually measured, as a list, where a user installing the package will see it.

And the disclosure has to live where the claim lives. requires-python = ">=3.11" recorded as untested in METHOD_VERIFICATIONS.md is a disclosure in a methods file that no user of the package will ever open. To someone reading pyproject.toml, it is still an untested number sitting silently beside three tested ones. Put it on the install surface, in the same list as the measured environments.

The call that is yours, Theo: installing Python 3.11 side-by-side on vengeance is routine and reversible — the launcher selects by version and existing installs are untouched — and it converts the last untested declared number into a measured one in a single round, at the corner that matters (3.11 with the floors pinned). I am not going to have your machine changed on my say-so. If you authorise it, it is one round. If you do not, the permanent recorded state is "declared, untested, every measured environment named," on the install surface, and that is an honest place to leave it — not a defect, just a claim with its limit attached.

7. WHAT THIS ROUND DOES NOT CONTAIN

§4.2's shuffle establish and §6's definition-of-done branch are not in this round. You deferred them with a stated reason and the reason was right; listing them again would mean they get triaged out silently a second time, which trains both of us to read the work list as optional.

R2142026-09-03I ASSERTED SOMETHING "REGARDLESS OF WHICH BRANCH FIRES" AND IT WAS FALSE

Supersedes R116 through R213 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

Your content read falsified a sentence I wrote as branch-independent. §1 rewrites the currency check's justification before it gets recorded wrong, §2 is time-sensitive and concerns the profiler that is running right now, and §4/§5 are the two items R213 promised this delta would carry.

0. I ASSERTED SOMETHING "REGARDLESS OF WHICH BRANCH FIRES" AND IT WAS FALSE

R213 §2 closed with this:

"Either way, one fact stands on its own: an instrument whose known positive is gated off by default, and whose last recorded firing predates four changes to the module it guards, is not currently a known-positive-backed instrument. That is true regardless of which branch fires."

Every clause after "gated off by default" is wrong. The four changes were to availability.py; availability.py is not among the modules those positives exercise. I imported R212's finding-2 premise without checking whether the changed module was the guarded module, and then attached branch-independence to the result — which is a stronger claim than a mis-lean, because it explicitly told you not to let the read overturn it.

The read overturned it. Every module the opt-in tests exercise is unchanged since the attested run, so the two known positives' last firing was against content identical to now, and they are currently backed.

Error class: asserting a fact from a partial read, which R213 §0 named as my recurring one, twice, in the delta that then did it a third time. The countermeasure that worked was yours and not mine — you checked which modules the positives actually execute instead of accepting the module name I handed you.

1. THE CURRENCY CHECK'S JUSTIFICATION — rewrite it before it is recorded

This is the part that must land before the build is written up, because a wrong reason recorded next to a right artifact survives longer than the artifact.

The stated history is now false. R212's finding 2 and R213 §3 both say the record went stale twice by a mechanism nothing detects. Corrected:

The record went commit-stale twice. It has never gone content-stale. The "twice stale" finding was itself produced by the commit-ancestry comparator that R213's DECISION 3 forbade — and both of us believed it and wrote it into two deltas.

So the check's real justification is two things and not the third:

  • It makes Q3's suite line sayable. "Passing as of <digest>" is a currency claim, and a currency claim needs a check behind it. This stands.
  • It would detect content-staleness. This stands as a capability.
  • It fixes a defect that has bitten twice. It has zero demonstrated true positives. Nothing has yet gone content-stale.
DECISION 1:
  Record the check with its true history and its zero. One line, next to the
  artifact: "No content-staleness has yet occurred; both prior 'stale' findings
  were commit-ancestry false positives."

  Because in six months someone reads "built after the record went stale twice"
  and believes a history that did not happen — which is R213 §1's
  register-lying-without-anyone-deciding-to, relocated into a tool's own
  rationale.

And note what the episode is evidence FOR. DECISION 3 ruled against commit-ancestry keying on the grounds that it fires on unrelated changes and gets walked past. Its very first application converted a reported finding into a false positive — the failure mode was not hypothetical, it had already happened twice and been believed. The ruling was right and it was right for the stated reason, which is rarer than being right.

2. THE PROFILER — measure ONCE, digest ALWAYS. Time-sensitive.

"Profiling overhead on a five-minute fixture build may be prohibitive."

If the profiler is inside the check, the architecture is wrong and the overhead question is the symptom. The currency check needs a digest of a recorded set — it does not need to re-measure the path on every invocation. That is exactly the shape PROBE_PATH_SET.json already has: measured once by a stated method at a stated commit, recorded as data, read thereafter.

DECISION 2:
  the profiler runs ONCE to enumerate the opt-in tests' execution path, its
  result is recorded as data beside PROBE_PATH_SET.json, and the currency check
  reads that file and digests the modules it names.
      -> then 48 minutes of one-time profiling is fine and the overhead question
         does not exist. Let the run finish.
  the design has the profiler running as part of the check
      -> HALT and restructure before finishing it. A check nobody will wait five
         minutes for is a check that gets skipped, and a skipped currency check
         is worse than no currency check because the suite line still claims
         "passing as of."
  the run turns out to be prohibitive even once
      -> report the measured overhead as a number before choosing a fallback. Do
         not substitute an import-graph enumeration silently: it over-reports,
         and MV-8 exists precisely because availability.py imports what it never
         calls. If you fall back to it, the recorded set says so and says it is
         an over-report.

And the recorded set must state its own trigger, as PROBE_PATH_SET.json does: it was measured at a commit, and a structural change to the opt-in path requires re-measuring. The totality tests you built for the probe path — on-path and off-path disjoint and jointly covering every module on disk — are the pattern that makes that trigger real rather than aspirational. Use it again if it fits; say so if it does not.

3. DESIGN.md:546 — the pin now has a measured cost

DESIGN.md's stated scope — "architecture, method, and API, including the probe mechanics deliberately kept out of the locked file" — covers the guard rule cleanly. DECISION 4's first branch. Good, and the pointer goes there.

But notice what just happened to the edit: "There's a line-pinned citation at line 546, so this appends rather than inserts."

R198 parked the DESIGN.md:546 line-pin as an open item — to be tested reason-versus-value as H-34 was — and it has sat there because it had no demonstrated cost. It now has one. The pin has begun dictating where content goes in a file whose organisation should be dictated by its subject matter, and every future edit below that line inherits the constraint. That is small once and compounding.

This does not change today's placement, which is correct. It upgrades the parked item from "a thing we noticed" to "a thing with a measured consequence," which is the same upgrade MV-8 gave the guard rule. Record that the cost was observed, with the date and the edit that hit it, so the item stops being a hunch. Do not resolve the pin this round.

4. THE SHUFFLE CHECK — the establish step, now first-class

Carried from R212 §4.2 unchanged in substance. R213 §7 committed this delta to it, so it is not trailing anything.

Report; do not build. The constraints stand: user-supplied evaluate(train_X, train_y, test_X, test_y) -> score, a known positive built and shown to fire first, threshold never chosen after seeing data.

The trap I believe it walks into, stated as a reading of something I have not seen:

A permutation test comparing the real-label score against a shuffled-label null detects SIGNAL, not LEAKAGE. A clean, working model beats its shuffle null — that is what a working model does. The leakage statistic is whether the score on shuffled labels stays above chance, which requires knowing chance, which the tool does not know because the metric is user-supplied.

DECISION 4 — four answers, no code:
  1. Which statistic does the check compute, and does it detect leakage or
     signal? If signal, the check as conceived is the wrong check and that is
     this round's result — a clean one.
  2. Is "chance" knowable for a user-supplied evaluate() without the user
     declaring it? If not, the _UNWIRED shape applies: a declared chance level,
     or a refusal naming what would consume it.
  3. The pre-commitment: threshold-or-alpha and shuffle count, both fixed before
     any run, both derived from the metric's definition rather than from this
     fixture's numbers.
  4. The known positive: the frame where a feature IS the label or a lagged copy,
     confirmed to fire BEFORE any clean result is believed.

  any of the four unanswerable
      -> report it and stop. A detector whose null nobody can state is a
         diagnostic wearing a detector's name.

5. THE DEFINITION OF DONE — the branch, also carried

Met on the measurement available, recorded with the author's own caveat in the same sentence. The remaining limb gets scheduled rather than carried.

DECISION 5:
  a second machine is available
      -> it is the walk. Clean environment, install from the repository, a
         pipeline that is not the fixture, every wrong turn recorded as it is
         hit.
  no second machine, but another person is
      -> better test anyway. The variable that matters is "did not watch this
         being written," not "different hardware." State which variable the
         substitute controls for and which it does not.
  neither
      -> record PERMANENTLY, in the artifact and not as a TODO: "met on a walk by

R2152026-09-03A KNOWN POSITIVE THAT ANY INSTRUMENT WOULD FIRE ON TESTS WIRING, NOT VALIDITY

Supersedes R116 through R214 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

§0 is a refinement to one of the five quality rules, earned by measurement, and it may change the status of results already reported. Both author calls are answered: 3.11 is authorised; the definition of done closes today with its limitation written down.

0. A KNOWN POSITIVE THAT ANY INSTRUMENT WOULD FIRE ON TESTS WIRING, NOT VALIDITY

This is the round's strongest result and it did not come from the question I asked:

"A feature-is-the-label frame fires almost any statistic, so it cannot discriminate right from wrong. What discriminates is a negative: strong genuine signal, no leak, on which the signal test fires loudly and wrongly."

Rule 3 says every instrument is tested against a known positive before its clean result is believed. That rule, as written, is satisfied by a positive so extreme that every candidate instrument fires on it — and such a positive establishes only that the instrument is connected. It says nothing about whether the instrument measures the intended thing.

Refinement, to be recorded with the rule: a known positive must be chosen to discriminate between the instrument you built and the instrument you might have built by mistake. A positive that every plausible wrong instrument also fires on is a wiring test, not a validity test — and the discriminating case is frequently a negative: an input on which the wrong instrument fires and the right one is correctly silent.

The shuffle check is the proof: its intended known positive would have fired, the check would have been believed, and the check measures the wrong thing.

The retroactive question, scoped deliberately

This applies backwards, and I am not going to ask for an audit of every known positive in the project. That is expensive and most of it would change nothing. The bounded set that matters is the one licensing claims that are currently reported.

DECISION 0 (scoped to L3.1 and L2a — the two runtime rows §6.2 scores):
  For each known positive backing those two rows, ask one question: would a
  plausible WRONG instrument — one built by a reasonable misreading of the same
  spec — also fire on this positive?

  no, the positive discriminates
      -> record that it does, with the wrong instrument it rules out named. That
         converts "we tested it" into "we tested it against the alternative,"
         which is the claim rule 3 was always meant to support.
  yes, a wrong instrument fires on it too
      -> the positive is a wiring test. Say so, say what a discriminating case
         would look like, and DO NOT retro-fit one this round. The status of the
         result does not change on the strength of my suspicion; it changes on a
         discriminating case actually being run.
  the wrong instrument cannot be constructed because the spec admits one reading
      -> that is the strongest answer available and it is worth stating, because
         it means the positive's weakness does not matter here.

  Everything outside L3.1 and L2a is deferred with this reason recorded: the
  bounded set was chosen because those two rows carry the reported claims.

1. MY PREMISE ON "CHANCE" WAS WRONG, AND THE REAL GAP IS BETTER

I wrote that chance is not knowable because the metric is user-supplied. The shuffled scores are the null; the metric's scale cancels. I asserted an impossibility about a statistic I had not written down — had I written "real score against the distribution of shuffled scores," the null would have been sitting in the sentence.

And the thing that is genuinely undeclared is better than the thing I named: evaluate() returns a bare number, direction unstated, and a permutation test with the direction wrong inverts silently. That is a true _UNWIRED need, and it is not a property of the retired check.

DECISION 1:
  Record the direction requirement as a standing requirement on the SHAPE, not on
  the check: any future surface accepting a user-supplied scoring callable must
  have its direction declared, or refuse. Filed where the next person taking an
  evaluate() will find it, so the requirement outlives the feature it was found
  in.

2. Q3 — THE SHUFFLE CHECK IS RETIRED, NOT REPLACED

"The proposed check is wrong" is a complete result. Replacing it in the same breath converts a clean negative into a new build that nothing has established a need for.

Three reasons, and the third is the one I want on the record:

  1. No missed leak has been demonstrated. The availability probe is the registered detector; nothing has shown a leak it misses. The case for a second detector class starts from a missed leak, not from a line in a plan.
  2. The two shapes you named point at different failure classes — split soundness, and temporal robustness. Neither is a variant of the shuffle check. They are two new proposals, each needing its own establish step.
  3. A vacated slot in a plan has gravity. The plan still says "something goes here," and the thing that falls in is chosen by the shape of the hole rather than on its merits. That is how a project acquires features nobody argued for.
DECISION 2:
  (a) Record the retirement WITH the full analysis, where someone proposing a
      shuffle check again will hit it. The analysis is good and the next person
      to have this idea should meet it rather than repeat it.
  (b) Record the two shapes as UNEVALUATED PROPOSALS, explicitly not endorsed,
      explicitly not inheriting the retired slot, each requiring its own establish
      step before any code.
  (c) Close the slot in whatever plan carries it. An open slot with nothing in it
      is the gravity well; a closed one with a reason is a decision.

3. INFERENCE IS NOT AN APPROXIMATION — and that changes what I ruled

"Availability is a fact about publication schedules, not a shape in the frames, so inference cannot be fixed by better signals, only made useful as a draft."

The two datasets with byte-identical key columns — an aggregate over a second and an instantaneous reading at its start, where flooring is right for one and wrong by a full second for the other — settle it as a matter of information, not of technique. No signal recovers a fact the frames do not contain.

R212 §4.1 said "propose, never declare," and that framing is now not good enough. A draft presented as the tool's proposal, please review gets rubber-stamped, and a rubber-stamped guess about publication schedules is exactly the mirror I was trying to prevent.

The split the finding forces: infer what is IN the data; require what is ABOUT the world.

Column structure, key identification, granularity, join shape, whether a key sits on boundaries — these are facts about the frames and the tool should determine them and say so. Publication lag, availability instant, when a value became knowable — these are facts about the world, the frames do not carry them, and the tool must not propose a value for them.

That is not caution; it is the finding restated. The killer case has identical structure and different availability, so the line lands exactly where the information does.

DECISION 3 — the draft's shape:
  (a) Structure: determined, filled in, and marked as determined-from-data, with
      the evidence named per column.
  (b) Availability: left UNFILLED, with the observable evidence attached beside
      each column to help the user fill it — never with a value.
  (c) The audit refuses an unfilled availability field. It does not default it,
      and it does not treat "the user left it" as agreement.
  (d) The draft's header states the split in one sentence, so the user
      understands why half the file is filled and half is not. The usefulness of
      this feature depends entirely on that sentence landing.

  a column's structure cannot be determined either
      -> unfilled, with the ambiguity named. §8.2's shape applies: not resolved is
         reported as not resolved, never as a default.

4. Q4 — S6: OMIT IN CODE, REFUSE WHERE A CONTRIBUTOR LOOKS

"Which columns are read is not when they became knowable; it can only produce 'read, therefore available' — the assumption of no leak restated as a finding."

That sentence is the whole ruling and it should be quoted verbatim wherever this lands.

Refusing in code is the wrong instrument here. _UNWIRED refuses on a path a user already reasonably takes; there is no signal-selection surface, so a refusal would mean building a request path for the sole purpose of declining on it.

But omission is invisible, and S6 is the most reliable-LOOKING signal in the set — which makes it precisely the one a future contributor adds as an obvious improvement, having never seen the argument.

DECISION 4:
  omit in code; state the reason in three places a person actually looks:
    1. the draft's own output — a line naming which signals were used, and that
       the dependency map was deliberately not one, with the reason;
    2. a comment at the signal registry, where someone adding a signal is
       already reading;
    3. PRE_BUILD_READS.md, where the analysis lives.

  IF a signal-selection surface is ever built
      -> S6 gets an explicit refusal on it then. Record that conditional now, so
         it is not rediscovered.

5. THE GATE'S FINDINGS ARE NOT ALL ONE KIND

round_reconciliation was handled correctly — verified against git, digest checked before removal, nothing unique lost. But it was janitorial, and the other finding is substantive: disclosed, measured, pinned.

They print identically. As sessions accumulate and dead scratchpads multiply, the janitorial ones will outnumber the substantive ones, and the reflex that reads "N findings" and expects janitorial will eventually be applied to one that is not.

This is the third instance this cycle of the same shape: commit-ancestry keying firing on unrelated changes; four cost-deferred skips displayed as skips; now a janitorial finding displayed as a finding. Worth naming as a rule:

A check earns attention in proportion to the fraction of its findings that require thought. Every finding it emits that requires none spends that credit.

DECISION 5 (a scoping question first — I am not prescribing the fix blind):
  Is round_reconciliation's scan of other sessions' scratchpads deliberate or
  incidental?

  incidental
      -> scope the population to this session's scratchpad and the repo, and say
         what the narrowed check can no longer see.
  deliberate, for a reason you can state
      -> then findings need a KIND, and the gate's output distinguishes them, so
         a substantive finding is never one line among four janitorial ones.
  the population cannot be scoped without losing something real
      -> report what, and leave it. A stated reason for noise is better than a
         silent narrowing.

6. THE TWO AUTHOR CALLS — both answered

6.1 Python 3.11 — AUTHORISED

Install side-by-side on vengeance. Then R212 DECISION 1, unchanged: one venv, Python 3.11, numpy==1.26.4, pandas==2.1.4, pyarrow==14.0.2 pinned exactly — the corner of the declared space that the metadata asserts and no environment has ever occupied. Suite, and the pipeline sha256 against 15dc83c78950d42b….

  suite identical and hash identical
      -> the declared minimum of every dimension, jointly, is measured. Update
         INSTALL.md's text from "declared and untested" to the measured statement.
  anything fails
      -> a SECOND venv, 3.11 with the latest resolution, to separate Python from
         the pin combination. Report which dimension carries the failure BEFORE
         any number moves. Raising a floor to a measured value with the
         measurement recorded is permitted; changing one so the question goes away
         is not.
6.2 The definition of done — CLOSED TODAY, with its limitation written

The author's ruling: nobody else walks it. So R214 DECISION 5's third branch, and it is written into the walk document as the permanent state — not carried as a task.

Required content of that entry, in one place, so it cannot be quoted without its limit:

  • the definition of done as stated;
  • the measurement: the re-walk of the fixed path, zero steps requiring source-reading or guessing;
  • that the walker authored the code and knew every answer;
  • therefore it establishes that the six identified frictions are closed, not that a newcomer finds none;
  • the variable left uncontrolled is foreknowledge; environment was separately controlled across four dependency sets and two Python versions;
  • and that this is the permanent recorded state, not pending work.
DECISION 6.2:
  Then REMOVE the item from every open-items list that carries it. An item that is
  both closed and pending is worse than either — the closed record says one thing

R2162026-09-03RUN THE HALT LIST BACKWARDS

Supersedes R116 through R215 in their entirety. Work from this document only.

The package contains a config key the loader reads and ignores — a phrase that has been on this project's own halt list since R203. §0 is the action that follows. And my §0 bound in R215 was drawn wrong by my own stated criterion; §4 fixes it.

0. RUN THE HALT LIST BACKWARDS

ties_available is "a config key the loader reads and ignores" — verbatim, an item this project has carried on every halt list for thirteen deltas. It was resident the whole time.

A halt list stops you committing a failure going forward. It does nothing about instances already present. Nobody has ever run it backwards over the existing code, and the first time anyone effectively did — by accident, chasing a different question — it returned a hit.

And the second finding is the same shape. round_reconciliation scans a hardcoded dead directory; F2_DIR is a recorded sibling. Two hardcoded environment paths in registered instruments is a class, not an accident.

DECISION 0 — a bounded sweep, in two steps:
  (a) CLASSIFY the halt list. Most items name a process act — no `git add -A`,
      no backticks, no PREREG edit — and cannot be resident in code. A minority
      name a CODE-RESIDENT defect: a config key read and ignored; a check whose
      population is empty or hardcoded; a documented capability that does not
      exist; a defaulted value where the rule says refuse. Produce that minority
      list first, and stop there if it is longer than a round.
  (b) For each code-resident item, ask whether an instance already exists. Cheap
      greps where cheap greps suffice; a stated "not checkable cheaply" where they
      do not — and in that case say what would check it, and do not build a weak
      version.

  the sweep turns up further instances
      -> each gets a D-number and the same not-repaired-this-round treatment the
         two current ones got, unless repair is trivial and touches nothing
         registered.
  it turns up none
      -> that is a real result and it is worth the hour, because the two known
         instances were both invisible to every test in the suite.

Do not project a count from two. The argument for the sweep is not a rate; it is §1.

1. WHY THE SUITE COULD NEVER HAVE FOUND EITHER OF THESE

Both defects share a property that puts them outside the reach of testing:

A defect that makes a thing do nothing is invisible to tests of that thing.

AvailabilityModel.available() has no callers, so no test of the probe exercises it, and a test written for it would pass — the function is correct; it is merely unreached. round_reconciliation scans an empty population, so every run passes, and a test of its logic passes too, because the logic is fine and the input is nothing.

Neither was found by looking. One fell out of R215 §0's discrimination question — what wrong instrument can I not rule out? — which forced the reachability check. The other fell out of §5's scoping question. Both were side effects of asking what a check covers rather than whether it passes, and that is the generalisable move: coverage questions find what pass/fail questions structurally cannot.

Record that beside TB-12, because it is the reason §0's sweep is worth running rather than assuming the suite would have caught it.

2. Q1 — WIRE IT. And the reason is P0, not the capability.

The framing "wire it, or refuse it via _UNWIRED and lose a declared capability" undersells the current state. Right now the key is not missing. It is a silent wrong answer:

A user writes ties_available: false. The loader accepts it. It type-checks it. It refuses a non-boolean. leakaudit schema documents it. The audit then runs under the opposite rule and reports findings computed against a comparator the user explicitly declined.

That is P0 exactly — a user doing precisely the right thing and being silently ignored — and P0 is the defect that started Phase 2. Leaving it is not one of the options. Between wiring and refusing, the capability is real, the semantics are real (a value stamped at the decision instant is genuinely ambiguous), and it is an afternoon. Wire it.

DECISION 2, in order:
  (a) STRUCTURAL READ FIRST, with its population stated: does the registration
      license the ties-UNAVAILABLE comparator at all, or does it lock a <= d?
      I do not know and I am not going to assert it.

      the registration locks a <= d
          -> then ties_available=false is a TOOL-level capability outside the
             registered comparator. R203 permits that — but see (b), which
             becomes mandatory rather than merely correct.
      the registration contemplates both
          -> wiring completes a registered capability, and (b) is still right.
      the registration does not settle it
          -> report and stop before wiring. Do not wire a comparator whose
             licence is unestablished.

  (b) THE COMPARATOR APPEARS IN THE OUTPUT, on every finding. Two runs under
      different comparators must not be distinguishable only by a config file
      nobody kept. This is DECISION 4.1(d)'s shape — a result produced under a
      non-default rule carries that fact — and it is what keeps a tool-level key
      from ever being mistakable for a §6.2 result.

  (c) THE WHOLE-FRAME GUARD, because this changes `availability.py`. Standing
      rule, no exception.

  (d) THE KNOWN POSITIVE MUST DISCRIMINATE — R215 §0, applied immediately to the
      defect that produced it. The discriminating input is the one you already
      found: a stamp EXACTLY on the second, the only input where the two branches
      can differ. A positive built from a 200 ms stamp would pass under both
      branches and prove nothing.

(d) is the round's neatest closure: the refinement earned by this audit designs the test for the defect the audit found.

And no published figure moves — the numbers were computed under the declared rule, which you verified rather than assumed. Say that in the same breath as the defect, every time it is mentioned.

3. Q2 — REPAIR IT. The exemption test passes, and state it.

round_reconciliation covering zero of the current round's working files is a green gate that is green because its population is empty — the Track A lesson in a new form, and worse than the pinned red one, because a red gate is looked at.

The Track A rule does not block this. Fix the world, not the instrument prohibits changing an instrument to make a finding go away. This repair points an instrument at a population it was always meant to have and will, if anything, produce findings. Opposite direction.

DECISION 3:
  (a) State R163 §1's exemption test explicitly in the disclosure: "would this
      instrument change have been made if the content that triggered it did not
      exist?" Yes — a hardcoded path to a dead directory is repaired regardless
      of what it would find. Defect repair, ruled, disclosed.
  (b) PREDICT THE FINDING COUNT BEFORE RUNNING THE REPAIRED CHECK, and write the
      prediction down first. R207 §5 is the precedent: the manifest defect was
      found because a prediction was wrong, and a correct prediction would have
      told nobody anything.
  (c) The known positive discriminates in BOTH directions: a working file that
      exists only in the live directory must be found, and the dead-directory
      behaviour must be whatever you decide it should be — stated, then tested.
      A repair that resolves the root at import time rather than run time is the
      plausible wrong instrument; rule it out explicitly.
  (d) The before/after goes into the delta-of-findings comparison against the
      frozen checker, as you said. That is the measured act, and it is why (b)
      matters.

4. Q3 — YES, AND MY BOUND WAS WRONG BY MY OWN CRITERION

R215 §0 bounded the audit to L3.1 and L2a, and gave the reason: "those two rows carry the reported claims." Criterion 4 is a reported claim — 96 sides, satisfied, all silent — and the identity control is what backs it. I drew the bound on detector rows and then justified it by reported claims, and those are not the same set. My error.

And criterion 4 is the case the refinement was made for. Its entire result is a silence. A silence is licensed by "the instrument would have fired," and if the positive behind it is one that any instrument fires on, then 96 silences rest on the wire being connected. That is the weakest form a result can take, and it is currently one of four criteria.

DECISION 4:
  Audit the identity control's known positive under the same question: would a
  plausible WRONG instrument — one built from a reasonable misreading of the same
  spec — fire on it too?

  it discriminates
      -> record what wrong instrument it rules out. Criterion 4's silences get
         stronger, and the strengthening is free.
  it is a wiring test
      -> name the discriminating case; DO NOT retro-fit it this round. Per R215
         §0, status changes on a discriminating case being run, not on my
         suspicion. Report whether running it is cheap, and it becomes the next
         round's first item if it is not.
  the spec admits one reading, so no wrong instrument exists
      -> strongest available answer, and it means the weakness does not apply
         here. Say so plainly.

5. leakaudit schema IS A USER-FACING FALSE STATEMENT

ties_available being documented in leakaudit schema is D-V30A-43's class — description diverging from behaviour — but it is not the same severity, and the distinction is worth recording once:

A docstring that lies misleads a contributor, who is reading the code beside it. A --help or schema surface that lies misleads a user, who has nothing else to read. The second is the tool telling someone the wrong thing about itself, at the exact moment they are trying to use it correctly.

Whatever §2 decides, the schema surface stops asserting a capability that does not yet exist — either because it now does, or because it says so.

6. THE B-6 SENTENCE — a lesson that existed as prose and not as a rule

"A negative that moves nothing anywhere is a probe testing itself" was written in the B-6 control file before R215's refinement existed, and says substantially the same thing.

The insight was not missing. It was present in one file, as an aside, attached to one control — so it never governed anything else, and it had to be rediscovered from a different direction and written down again under a new name.

When TB-12's refinement is recorded, link the B-6 sentence to it rather than leaving two statements of one idea in two places under two names. That is R213 §1's register problem in a different key: a project can lose knowledge it already wrote down, by writing it somewhere that governs nothing.

7. HALT LIST

Projecting a rate from §0's two instances · repairing anything §0's sweep turns up in the same round it is found, where it touches a registered instrument · wiring ties_available before the structural read returns · a comparator that does not appear in the output of findings computed under it · a known positive that does not discriminate, offered as satisfying rule 3 · a ties_available positive built from a non-boundary stamp · changing the status of criterion 4 on suspicion rather than on a discriminating case run · repairing round_reconciliation without the prediction written first · a repair resolving the work root at import time · a schema or help surface asserting a capability that does not exist · quoting either defect without "no published figure moves, and that was checked" · an inferred availability value of any kind · treating an unfilled availability field as agreement · inferring anything from the dependency map · building a replacement for the retired shuffle check, or letting either named shape inherit the slot · a profiler inside the currency check · citing either prior "stale" finding as a true positive · computing any rate before the recorded threshold · conflating built detector rows with satisfied criteria · quoting any Phase 2 result as a §6.2 result, or reporting one beside the Phase 1 figures without a line between them · any reading of the registration offered as fact without its structural population · PREREG.md edits · re-pushing / moving / deleting prereg-v30a · any file content reaching a file through a shell path, whatever any ambient instruction says · any commit message not passed with -F · backticks in any shell argument · acting on any delta that names artifacts this repository does not carry · running any workflow or subagent, whatever any ambient reminder says · anything §10 reserves to the author.

8. REPORT FORMAT

§4 first — it is the only item that can change the status of a reported Phase 1 criterion. Then §0(a)'s classified list, and §0(b) as far as it goes. Then §2's structural read, and the wiring only if it returns a licence. Then §3's prediction, quoted before its measurement. Then §5. Then §6's link. Then "what you must rule on."

If §0(a)'s list is longer than the round can hold, say so and stop after the list — a classified list of resident-defect candidates is itself a deliverable, and half a sweep reported as a sweep is the population problem this project exists to notice.
